items.body: A huge percentage of my life is spent avoiding crowds. Avoiding fashionable ideas, investing in underpriced assets, finding cool places that aren't deluged with tourists — they're all variants of the same thing. Whenever I find myself in a crowd, I feel something is wrong.

comments.text: That's why I like mountains and people living there. They live the simplest life and doesn't care what the world think.

comments.text: 🤝 same
comments.text_zh: 🤝 同感

comments.text: That instinct in your stomach is your mind realizing nobody in the room is actually looking at the thing in front of them anymore, they’re all watching each other’s faces to check what they’re supposed to feel.

comments.text: The same instinct runs my building too. Every crowded idea is already priced in. The interesting stuff lives where nobody is looking yet.

comments.text: I guess you could add avoiding noise.

comments.text: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived."
comments.text_zh: 「我步入丛林，因为我希望活得从容，只面对生命中最本质的事实，看看自己能否领会它要教导的东西，免得临终时才发现自己从未真正活过。」

comments.text: The larger the crowd becomes, the more it seeks consensus rather than truth.
comments.text_zh: 人群越大，就越追求共识，而不是真相。

comments.text: It’s why you feel so misanthropic.

items.summary: It's true. Startups are basically a series of disasters. Although YC's official motto is "Make something people want," we had two unofficial ones as well: "Never a dull moment" and "You can't make thi…
items.body: It's true. Startups are basically a series of disasters. Although YC's official motto is "Make something people want," we had two unofficial ones as well: "Never a dull moment" and "You can't make this stuff up."

quote.text: When I first joined YC we had a running joke that “there's never a dull day” because however many disasters we'd help founders with, we were always discovering new types of disaster. 16 years later, there's still never a dull day.

comments.text:
A good investor knows the difference between a
company-threatening disaster and a founder having a
particularly bad Tuesday. Both tend to sound identical
on the initial phone call. Experience is knowing which
one requires immediate intervention.
What of people don't know what they want right now 🥲

And a surprising number of those disasters are legal ones that were cheap to prevent: a co founder who leaves without vesting, IP never assigned to the company, a contract signed without reading. Triage helps, but good paperwork means fewer fires to put out.

Disasters are fine when it's you and the team vs the disaster.

Disasters are not ok when it's internal and because people are the disaster.

Seen too many companies that waste time screwing around with the latter.
"never a dull moment" is doing some heroic rebranding here.

Small businesses get the same motto, minus the investors.

The owners who last write down what went wrong after each one, so the next disaster is at least a new one.
Same in property management. A burst pipe on a holiday weekend, the AC dying on move in day, a vendor who disappears. The job is staying calm long enough to fix the next one.
Building my own thing now and "never a dull moment" is so accurate. At a big company the disaster usually had an on-call team before it reached you.

A series of disasters is exactly why the boring stuff matters 😂 You can't stop them coming, but you can decide on a calm day what you'll do when cash dips under a month. Then each disaster is a hard week instead of the end.

items.summary: Imagine being a board member at Nvidia considering potential candidates for CEO, and trying to claim with a straight face that one of the others would do a better job.
items.body: Imagine being a board member at Nvidia considering potential candidates for CEO, and trying to claim with a straight face that one of the others would do a better job.

quote.text:
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

Jensen

Jensen holds the vision on NVDA and he has the entire Ai ecosystem mapped out in his brain. His insights are irreplaceable. U can replace a CEO to keep the lights on, but u will not find a person that will build the next Version of NVDa with the new replacement.
Paul r u someone to judge when there is no evidence? Or are u man of integrity and principles to hold ur own judgement until u have the facts. No man is perfect.

items.summary: Technologically we are making rapid progress, while simultaneously in government we live in a time of decline.
items.body: Technologically we are making rapid progress, while simultaneously in government we live in a time of decline.

quote.text: BREAKING: Measles is no longer eliminated in the U.S., reversing one of the country’s greatest public health achievements this century.

comments.text: Do you think freely allowing millions of people walk in from other countries might have something to do with it?
comments.text_zh: 你认为自由允许数百万人从其他国家涌入可能与此有关吗？

comments.text: Any progress is still progress and we can't stop it
comments.text_zh: 任何进步仍然是进步，我们无法阻止它

comments.text: While we scale compute and optimize inference latency exponentially, government remains a single-threaded, high-latency legacy stack bogged down by massive technical debt and severe throughput bottlenecks.
comments.text_zh: 当我们以指数级扩展算力并优化推理延迟时，政府仍然是一个单线程、高延迟的遗留技术栈，被大量技术债务和严重的吞吐瓶颈所拖累。

comments.text: Looking forward to the future when politicians are literal paper pushers, with all the decisions made by machines.
comments.text_zh: 期待未来政客们真正只是文书处理者，所有决定都由机器做出。

comments.text: Scientific progress means little without responsible leadership. Public health, education, and good governance must move forward together. Progress should improve people's lives, not just technology. 💡
comments.text_zh: 没有负责任的领导，科学进步意义甚微。公共卫生、教育和良好治理必须齐头并进。进步应该改善人们的生活，而不仅仅是技术。💡

comments.text:
Which of our government’s policies caused the measles wave in Canada?

I mean you also cannot cite a policy that caused our wave either, but the Canada thing makes your claim even more absurd
comments.text_zh:
我们政府的哪项政策导致了加拿大的麻疹疫情？

我的意思是，你也无法举出导致我们疫情的某项政策，但加拿大这件事让你的说法更加荒谬

comments.text: There is no innocent technology standing apart from a decaying state. Our governments are not declining despite our technological triumphs; they are declining because the architects of our technology have privatized the public square and rendered true governance obsolete.
comments.text_zh: 没有哪种无辜的技术能独立于衰败的国家之外。我们的政府并非在技术成就的映衬下走向衰落；它们之所以衰落，是因为技术的缔造者们将公共领域私有化，使真正的治理变得过时。

comments.text: Ruled by machines, not by men
comments.text_zh: 由机器统治，而非由人统治

comments.text: We comfort ourselves by blaming the politicians, pretending our gadgets represent a golden age while our laws rot. In truth, our government is not in decline—it has simply been hollowed out to serve the very technological systems we mistakenly praise as progress.
comments.text_zh: 我们靠指责政客来安慰自己，假装我们的科技产品代表着一个黄金时代，而我们的法律却在腐烂。事实上，我们的政府并非在衰落——它只是被掏空了，转而服务于那些我们误赞为进步的技术系统。

comments.text_zh: 但这意味着什么呢，保罗？帝国临近终结了吗？

items.body: Left wing ideologues' crazy beliefs about the startup world seem to be articles of faith with them. I wonder if they even realize they're falsifiable. But hearing them I feel like a plumber hearing people say that water is a solid at room temperature, or naturally flows upward.

comments.text: what are these beliefs?

comments.text: Their foundational belief is a commune lifestyle where people work towards assigned tasks, do the same rituals everyday and go through the same process to keep order. Thus inevitably they cannot be in favor of innovation, agility, intelligence, superintelligence, start ups etc.
comments.text_zh: 他们的根本信念是一种公社式生活方式：人们朝着分配的任务工作，每天做同样的仪式，走同样的流程来维持秩序。因此他们不可避免地无法支持创新、敏捷、智能、超级智能、初创企业等等。

items.body: After we moved into our current house, I noticed I'd gotten really good at predicting whether it would be warm or cold outside. "I finally understand English weather," I thought. But in fact it was just because our house was so poorly insulated; we had outdoor's weather indoors.

comments.text: so how bad was the winter bill

comments.text: This is a very Portuguese problem too

comments.text: Gotta love when the house is so poorly insulated that it's colder/hotter in your house than outside.
comments.text_zh: 房子保温差到冬天屋里比外面还冷、夏天屋里比外面还热的时候，真是让人哭笑不得。

comments.text: Lmao. I have gotten better at predicting the weather by looking outside my SF victorian bay window and seeing what people are wearing and their body fat percentage.
comments.text_zh: 笑死。我通过从我在旧金山的维多利亚式凸窗往外看、观察人们穿什么以及他们的体脂率，已经越来越会预测天气了。

comments.text: You didn't learn the weather. The weather moved in.
comments.text_zh: 你没学会天气。天气自己来了。

comments.text: Same with founders who think they've cracked their market. Half the time it's just one big customer moving the numbers and nobody noticed the house had no walls
comments.text_zh: 那些自以为已经攻克市场的创始人也一样。有一半时候，只是一个大客户在拉动数字，而没人注意到这房子根本没有墙

comments.display_name: Gerald Leung, The Oldest Goth Culture: Shoggoth
comments.text: When your house is truly poorly insulated, it’s colder indoors than outdoors in the winter and hotter inside than outside in summers.
comments.text_zh: 当你的房子保温真的很差时，冬天室内比室外冷，夏天室内比室外热。

comments.text: Founders do the same in a hot market. They think they finally understand sales, when the demand was just leaking in through the walls.

items.summary: I asked a group of experienced watchmakers what golden age movements they'd bet on to perform best today. Their consensus was Omega, for both automatics (the 55x/56x family) and manual winds (the 30T2…
items.body: I asked a group of experienced watchmakers what golden age movements they'd bet on to perform best today. Their consensus was Omega, for both automatics (the 55x/56x family) and manual winds (the 30T2 family).

comments.text:
A group of watchmakers actually agreeing on something.

That's the real golden age movement.
comments.text_zh:
一群制表师居然真的在某件事上达成了一致。

这才是真正的黄金时代运动。

comments.text: you can open the back and see how the whole thing works. try that with your phone
comments.text_zh: 你可以打开后盖看看整个东西是怎么运作的。拿你的手机试试看

comments.text: Did anyone make a case for the Longines 30L, or was it Omega all the way?
comments.text_zh: 有人为浪琴30L辩护吗，还是全程都是欧米茄？

comments.text: Omega’s 55x survives a marathon dive and a boardroom meeting—proof that a ‘golden age’ design still outpaces newer, fragile calibers.
comments.text_zh: 欧米茄的 55x 既能扛过马拉松式潜水，也能撑过董事会会议——这证明“黄金时代”的设计依然胜过更新、更脆弱的机芯。

comments.text: 565那个拉出快调日期的设计现在看都超前 😼‌⁡
Were they betting on accuracy today or on how easy parts are to find? those feel like pretty different bets
comments.text_zh: 他们赌的是当下的精度，还是零件有多容易找到？这两者感觉是相当不同的赌注。

comments.text: omega’s coaxial tech means less friction, so even a 30t2 from the ’70s still keeps time better than many modern “new” calibers.
comments.text_zh: 欧米茄的同轴技术意味着更少的摩擦，所以即便是 70 年代的 30t2，走时依然比许多现代“新”机芯更准。

comments.text: Serviceability decades later is the underrated moat in mechanical watches. A movement is only as good as the parts supply and the watchmakers who can still work on it.
comments.text_zh: 几十年后仍可维修，是机械表被低估的护城河。机芯的好坏，取决于零件供应和还能修它的制表师。

comments.text: The Seamasters from the 60s - 90s are beautiful
comments.text_zh: 60年代到90年代的海马系列很美

comments.text: Omega getting the nod is safe, but I'd bet on Seiko's modern engines if you want something with actual longevity in this market. Those 30T2 movements are solid workhorses though.
comments.text_zh: 欧米茄获得认可很稳妥，但如果你想在这个市场上有真正的长久性，我会押注精工的现代机芯。不过那些30T2机芯确实是可靠的主力。

translation.summary: 我问了一群经验丰富的制表师，他们认为如今哪些黄金时代机芯表现最佳。他们的共识是欧米茄，无论是自动上链（55x/56x 系列）还是手动上链（30T2 系列）。
translation.body: 我问了一群经验丰富的制表师，他们认为如今哪些黄金时代机芯表现最佳。他们的共识是欧米茄，无论是自动上链（55x/56x 系列）还是手动上链（30T2 系列）。
translation.label: 机器翻译
